areas.name: Typography
areas.definition: UI text is Geist; ids, paths, hashes and counts are Geist Mono. Body is text-sm, meta is text-xs, a product title is text-lg or text-xl. No text is smaller than text-xs (12 px), also not a menu group header, inline code, a badge or a chart label. Weights are 400 and 500 only: quiet text uses color or size, never a lighter weight. Sizes come from the Tailwind scale. Prose lines stay at about 75 characters or less. A title of two or more lines does not end with one word alone.

areas.name: Color tokens
areas.definition: Color comes from the house tokens: a zinc floor, a white primary, a teal accent. Red marks an error and the filled danger button of a confirm dialog. The dark UI has no large bright or saturated area: bright color is a small accent, such as a border, an icon or a dot, and a block has at most one teal edge or wash. A warning is a dark surface with a yellow or amber border and icon; a yellow fill with dark text is only for a small element, and only when it passes AA. An embedded editor, diff viewer or preview uses the dark theme. No indigo, no purple gradient, no second accent. Teal marks only the one real action in a dense list.

areas.name: Contrast
areas.definition: Text is readable on its surface: about 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text and icons. On a teal, red or amber slab, secondary text is a lighter stop of the same hue at full opacity, not white at reduced opacity. The text of an item that the user can click (a file tree, a nav list) is never so dim that it reads as disabled.

areas.name: Actions and affordance
areas.definition: Each control shows what it does: an icon tells its action, and the main action of a page has a label, not a lone + icon. A row that opens or expands is one pressable target across the full row, with a visible indicator such as a chevron; a chevron sits only on such a row. A row that does not open has no such indicator, and the controls in it look like controls.

areas.name: Dialog structure
areas.definition: A modal has a header, a body and a footer zone. It fits the viewport: the header and the footer stay in place, long content scrolls inside the body, and nothing is cut off at an edge of the screen. Each dialog and each step of a flow shows a way to close, cancel or go back, also when the screen would look cleaner without it. A dialog has one close control. In a wizard, it is one Close button at the bottom right, with no second Close or X at the top.

areas.name: Copy
areas.definition: Copy is plain and specific US English in every visible word, also a legend and a chart label (color, not colour). It tells the user what to do. Error copy gives the cause and a next step, and does not repeat the title. One row, card or dialog does not show the same text twice.

areas.name: Missing elements
areas.definition: An addition or deletion region adds or removes an element. A label, an icon, a status word, a control or the frame of a block does not disappear without a reason.

areas.name: Status
areas.definition: A status is a dot and its word. The color is on the dot; the words share one restrained text color. A dot pulses only while the work runs (running, syncing, indexing); a static state has a still dot.

areas.name: Overflow and truncation
areas.definition: Text, icons and focus rings fit their box. Nothing is cut off by a parent, nothing runs over a neighbor, and no element covers text. Long machine text (a URL, a token, an id, a stack trace, raw error text) never fills a message: a short sentence shows, and the detail is behind a disclosure or in a mono block with a capped height that scrolls. A signed URL or a value that looks like a secret never shows in full.

areas.name: Broken content
areas.definition: Labels, copy and field values show no rendering artifact: no undefined, null, NaN, [object Object], untranslated key, lorem ipsum or broken image. Each value is one that a real user can see: real-looking names, values and text, never random values, no debug output or raw serialized state of the UI, and no run of generated ids or names. A missing value shows a dash or a short empty text. A code or file preview that shows such text as its content is not broken.

areas.name: Spacing and alignment
areas.definition: Space and alignment follow the Gestalt principles of proximity and continuity. Space comes from the Tailwind scale. Text does not touch the edge of its button, card, pill or page. Long copy is left-aligned, never justified, and numbers are right-aligned with tabular figures.

qualities.name: Accessibility
qualities.definition: Every user can read and reach the UI. Text and icons are readable on their surface. The keyboard focus ring is readable and not clipped. A state never shows by color only: a status has its word, and an error has its text.

qualities.name: Clarity
qualities.definition: The user can tell what the screen is for, what each element is and does, and what to do next. The user can tell what a click on each area does: an area that reacts to a click looks pressable, and an area that looks pressable reacts. The current or next step of a task stands out from the steps around it. A button names its result with a verb and an object ("Save token", not "Submit"). Each form field has a visible label; a placeholder is only an example value. The screen shows what the task needs now; details, advanced options and the machine text that the user needs wait behind a disclosure.

qualities.name: Focus
qualities.definition: The page has at most one primary action: one filled white button. Other actions are outline, quiet or a link. Two equal choices at one rank can have the same style. A page that needs no action, such as an error page, a read-only view or a step of a popup, meets this quality.

qualities.name: Hierarchy
qualities.definition: One element leads: the title is the loudest ink, and the rest steps down. Hierarchy comes from weight and muted color, not from a size jump; neighbors and decorative icons are muted first. Each screen has a small budget of strong signals (a filled button, a bright color, a badge, a colored edge, an icon in a tile), and each one marks something that matters. When many elements carry the same strong weight, nothing leads, and the user cannot tell what to do first. Secondary chrome (legends, hints, help) is smaller and dimmer than the content and does not cover it.

qualities.name: Proximity
qualities.definition: The space inside a group is smaller than the space around it. An action sits next to the thing that it acts on.

qualities.name: Similarity
qualities.definition: The same meaning has the same look on the screen. Peer actions have the same weight.

qualities.name: Common region
qualities.definition: A surface, a frame or an inset holds each group. A card holds groups, not a second card. A local navigation (tabs, or a side list of sections) and the content that it switches read as one region: the navigation sits at the top or the leading edge of that content, not apart from it in empty space.

qualities.name: Figure–ground
qualities.definition: A card, a tile or a row stands off the page by its surface or by a clear border, not by a dim hairline. The content of a page reads as one figure on its ground: no block floats alone in a large empty area, and on a narrow screen the content fills the width, less the page margins.

qualities.name: Continuity
qualities.definition: Siblings share one edge and one marker axis. A child group steps in, and a different edge marks a different role. On a page, the title, the local navigation and the content blocks follow one column, and sibling blocks share one width unless their roles differ.

qualities.name: Prägnanz
qualities.definition: Each block reads in its simplest form: one state signal, quiet items inside, and space before a hairline.

qualities.name: Feedback and state
qualities.definition: Each state uses its house pattern. A region wait is a skeleton with the box of the loaded state. A process wait is the teal loader. An empty state is a short title, one sentence and one primary control. An error is an inline alert with its cause and a next step. The layout holds at its edges: a long name, zero, one or many items, an error and a loading state keep the structure of the screen.

qualities.name: Consistency
qualities.definition: Similarity holds across screens, so the change reuses the house primitives and patterns: one corner radius (rounded-md), the button variants, the status pill, the alert. No new font, hex color, corner treatment, shadow or card style.

qualities.name: Brand fit
qualities.definition: The surface reads as the ctxpipe Operate UI: dark zinc floor, white primary, teal accent, Geist type, monospace for ids, paths, hashes and counts. Large type and atmosphere stay on onboarding.

qualities.name: Density
qualities.definition: Operate density, as in chat, connectors and settings: tight, not landing-page air. Forms and prose keep a maximum width and start at the leading edge of the content column; data surfaces are full width.

qualities.name: Restraint
qualities.definition: No generic AI decoration: no gradient, gradient text, glass, grain, glow or grid on product chrome, no hero type, no four equal KPI tiles, no teal on every row, no badge stacked above a title, no numbers on sections that are not a sequence, no icon tile above the heading of an empty state, no glow or drop shadow on hover. A colored edge on one side of a block marks a state, such as a block that needs the user; a colored stripe that marks no state is decoration. An in-page card has no hard offset shadow and no wide black shadow; a dialog, popover, menu or toast keeps its house shadow. A blurred backdrop behind a modal, an uppercase heading that names a page section, and a status dot with its word are not decoration. These ctxpipe signatures are not tells: the mono uppercase .ctx-label as a section label in a dense panel (not as an eyebrow above a page title or a card heading), and corner crosses on a hero or summary card.
